cell.label: Complete initial evaluation. Start IV fluids: 1.0 L of 0.9% NaCl per hour initially
cell.path: Potassium: initial serum K+ under 3.3 mEq/L
Potassium: initial serum K+ 3.3 to under 5.0 mEq/L
Potassium: initial serum K+ 5.0 mEq/L or more

cell.label: Administer 0.9% NaCl (1.0 L/h) and/or plasma expanders
0.45% NaCl (4-14 mL • kg-1 • h-1) depending on state of hydration

Change to 5% dextrose with 0.45% NaCl and decrease insulin to 0.05-0.1 unit • kg-1 • h-1 to maintain serum glucose between 250 and 300 mg/dL until plasma osmolality is ≤315 mOsm/kg and patient is mentally alert
0.9% NaCl (4-14 mL • kg-1 • h-1) depending on state of hydration
0.1 unit • kg-1 • h-1 IV insulin infusion
Check serum glucose hourly. If serum glucose does not fail by at least 50 mg/dL in first hour, then double insulin dose hourly until glucose fails at a steady hour rate of 50-70 mg/dL

Check electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and glucose every 2-4 h until stable. After resolution of HHS, if the patient is NPO, continue IV insulin and supplement with SC regular insulin as needed. When the patient can eat, initiate SC insulin or previous treatment regimen and assess metabolic control. Continue to look for precipitating cause(s)
If initial serum K+ is <3.3 mEq/L, hold insulin and give 40 mEq K+ (2/3 as KCl and 1/3 KPO4) until K+ ≥3.3 mEq/L
If initial serum K+ ≥5.0 mEq/L, do not give K+ but check potassium every 2 h
If initial serum K+ ≥3.3 but <5.0 mEq/L, give 20-30 mEq K+ in each liter of IV fluid (2/3 as KCl and 1/3 KPO4) to keep serum K+ at 4-5 mEq/L

footnotes.footnote: BUN denotes blood urea nitrogen; IV: intravenous; NPO: L. nil per os (nothing by mouth); SC: subcutaneous.
Adapted from Kitabchi AE, Umpierrez GE, Murphy MB, et al. Hyperglycemic crises in diabetes. Diabetes Care 2004;27(suppl 1):S97.
